title: Are online reviews worth anything?

turns.speaker: Barry
turns.text: I booked a hotel on four point six stars and it was the worst room I've stayed in this decade.

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: Four point six is the danger zone, honestly. Nearly everything sits between four point two and four point eight now, so the number stopped carrying information.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: Compressed at the top because people leave five stars out of politeness and one star out of fury, and almost nothing in between.

turns.speaker: Barry
turns.text: So the average is two moods rather than a measurement.

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: And then there's the paid layer. Estimates of fake reviews on the big platforms run somewhere between four and fifteen per cent depending on who's counting.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: The fakes are getting harder to spot too. They used to be short and oddly enthusiastic. Now they're plausible paragraphs.

turns.speaker: Barry
turns.text: So is there anything left worth reading?

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: The three-star ones. Someone who thought about it for long enough to be ambivalent is usually the only person describing the actual room.

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: That's my rule too. And the count matters more than the score, because forty reviews is a sample and four is an anecdote.

turns.speaker: Barry
turns.text: What I can't get past is that the whole system replaced something that worked, which was a guidebook written by somebody paid to be honest.

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: It also replaced knowing nothing at all, though. Which is what most people had.

turns.speaker: Ines
turns.text: True. It's worse than the best thing it replaced and much better than the common one.

turns.speaker: Barry
turns.text: That's a fairer summary than mine.

points: Review averages cluster between about 4.2 and 4.8 stars, so the score carries little information.
Ines explains the compression: people leave five stars out of politeness and one out of anger, with little in between.
Estimates of fake reviews range from four to fifteen per cent, and fakes have become harder to detect.
Ines recommends reading three-star reviews, as ambivalent reviewers describe the actual experience.
Lena adds that the number of reviews matters more than the score, since forty is a sample and four is an anecdote.
Barry argues the system replaced paid honest guidebooks; Ines concludes it is worse than the best alternative but better than the common one of knowing nothing.
